strengths: The idea of building an indoor semantic occupancy dataset from in-the-wild YouTube house-tour videos is novel and well-motivated; the fully automatic pipeline (clip segmentation, Dust3R-based reconstruction, VFM semantic labeling, voxelization) addresses a real bottleneck (cost and privacy of indoor 3D annotation).
The superpixel/supervoxel contrastive distillation from vision foundation models is a reasonable, model-agnostic pre-training design for occupancy prediction and is clearly described.

Evaluation covers several settings: fine-tuning on NYUv2 and OccScanNet, annotation-efficient regimes (10%-100% labels), cross-dataset pre-training, and zero-shot transfer, giving a reasonably broad empirical picture.

Gains are most pronounced in the low-label regime (e.g., +5.25 mIoU on NYUv2 with 10% labels, +2.47 mIoU on OccScanNet with 1%), which is the practically relevant scenario for the claimed contribution, and a limitations discussion is provided.
weaknesses: Reproducibility of the central contribution is fundamentally undermined: the paper explicitly states the YouTube-Occ dataset 'will not be released in public,' and no code is provided. Since the dataset/pipeline is a primary contribution, the community cannot verify or build upon it, which is a serious issue for a Datasets/Benchmarks-style contribution.

The abstract claims 'state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on two popular benchmarks,' but the reported zero-shot results (9.95 mIoU on NYUv2, 4.61 mIoU on OccScanNet) are very low, presented without any baseline comparison, and the OccScanNet evaluation uses a non-standard re-split that prevents comparison to prior work. The claim is not supported by the evidence.

Supervised benchmark improvements over the Symphonies baseline are marginal (+1.04 mIoU on NYUv2, +0.30 mIoU on OccScanNet) with no error bars, repeated runs, or statistical significance tests, so it is unclear the gains exceed run-to-run variance. Some cross-dataset results are mixed (e.g., IoU at 50% on OccScanNet is worse than random init in Table 4).

The dataset is small for the 'web-scale data' narrative: only 14,592 frames from 651 clips, and the paper does not report how much raw video was collected/filtered, limiting conclusions about scalability of the pipeline.

Ablations are largely missing: the pre-training method's design choices (superpixel generation from SAN vs. other mask models, temperature, contrast formulation, DINOv2 vs. other embeddings) are not studied; a baseline distilling VFM features without superpixels is needed to isolate the contribution. Only one occupancy backbone (Symphonies) is tested, leaving the 'model-agnostic' claim unevidenced.

Label quality from pseudo-labeling (SAN semantics, heuristic metric scaling by assuming a 2.8 m wall height, z-up alignment) is not quantitatively validated against any ground truth, and no analysis of reconstruction/annotation error rates on the curated data is given.

Presentation issues: section cross-references are wrong (Section 4 refers to 'Section 3.1/3.2'), inconsistent dataset naming (YouTube-Occ vs. YouTube-OCC), typos ('collecte', 'Upon on this web dataset', 'Abstart'), which suggests insufficient polish.

strengths: The idea of building an automatic pipeline that converts in-the-wild YouTube house-tour videos into pseudo-annotated 3D semantic occupancy data (via Dust3R reconstruction, VFM-based semantic labeling, and voxelization) is a relevant and relatively unexplored direction for indoor occupancy prediction, where labeled data is scarce.

The VFM-assisted superpixel–supervoxel contrastive distillation is model-agnostic and evaluated on top of a strong baseline (Symphonies), with experiments covering both full-label and low-label (10/20/50/100%) settings on two benchmarks (NYUv2 and OccScanNet), plus cross-dataset pre-training and zero-shot transfer.
The paper is honest in its limitations section (dynamic objects ignored, dataset not released) and reports the rather weak zero-shot numbers transparently.
The most convincing result is the low-label regime on NYUv2 (e.g., +5.25% mIoU at 10% labels), which supports the claim that pre-training helps when annotations are scarce.
weaknesses: Overclaimed results. The abstract claims 'state-of-the-art zero-shot performance,' but the zero-shot results (9.95 mIoU on NYUv2, 4.61 on OccScanNet) are very weak, and no zero-shot baselines are compared to substantiate 'state-of-the-art.' The supervised SOTA gains are marginal: +1.04 mIoU on NYUv2 and only +0.30 mIoU / +0.25 IoU on OccScanNet, with no error bars or multiple seeds (explicitly admitted in the checklist), so these gains may not be statistically meaningful.

The central dataset contribution is not reproducible: the paper states YouTube-Occ 'will not be released in public.' For a paper whose main contribution is a new web dataset and pipeline, withholding the data (with no release plan, license, or YouTube ToS/consent discussion for scraped indoor footage of private homes) severely limits community impact and verifiability.

No ablation studies. The contributions of individual components (superpixel generation from SAN vs. alternatives, DINOv2 vs. other embedding models, temperature, majority voting, the heuristic 2.8m wall-height scaling, post-processing filters) are never isolated; there is also no comparison against any other pre-training/distillation method — only random initialization.

Limited novelty of the method: superpixel-based 2D-to-3D contrastive distillation closely follows prior work (e.g., Sautier et al. [28]), and VFM-to-3D distillation with DINOv2 features is well-established; the technical contribution is largely an adaptation to indoor occupancy rather than a new mechanism.

The constructed dataset is small for a 'web-scale' motivation: only 14,592 frames from 651 clips, and gains from YouTube-Occ pre-training are inconsistent on OccScanNet (IoU sometimes decreases, e.g., 55.77 vs. 55.90 at 50% labels), weakening the scalability claim.

Presentation issues that affect clarity: section numbering is wrong (Section 4.1/4.2 are referenced as 3.1/3.2), 'Tab. Fig. 5' and inconsistent 'YouTube-Occ/YouTube-OCC/YouTube-OCCc' naming, the contrastive loss sums from 0 to Q (off-by-one relative to the definition of Q superpixels), typos ('Abstart', 'collecte'), and inconsistent formatting of improvements (+1.04%mIoU).

The pseudo-label quality from the pipeline (Dust3R reconstruction errors, SAN segmentation errors on in-the-wild video, rough metric scaling) is never quantified (e.g., validation IoU of pseudo occupancy vs. any reference), making it hard to assess whether the pre-training benefits come from geometry, semantics, or simply extra data.

Ethical handling of the data is thin: the work uses scraped footage of real home interiors of identifiable houses, but the checklist provides no discussion of consent, YouTube terms of service, or safeguards beyond not releasing the data.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated direction: this appears to be the first work exploring in-the-wild YouTube videos for 3D semantic occupancy prediction, addressing the real data-scarcity problem in indoor scene understanding.

The fully automatic pipeline (video curation, Dust3R-based camera/depth estimation without intrinsics/extrinsics, VFM-based semantic labeling, voxelization) is a sensible and scalable design that removes the need for calibrated capture setups.

The proposed pre-training method is model-agnostic and technically reasonable: superpixel/supervoxel alignment via contrastive distillation leverages 2D foundation-model priors at an object level, mitigating pixel-level noise and scale ambiguity.

Consistent improvements across settings, particularly in the low-annotation regime: +5.25 mIoU with 10% labels on NYUv2 and +4.21 mIoU with 10% labels in cross-dataset pre-training, which supports the claim that web data provides useful 3D priors.
The paper is transparent about limitations (dynamic objects not handled, dataset not released) and provides reasonable experimental details (hardware, optimizers, schedules).
weaknesses: The primary dataset contribution (YouTube-Occ) will not be publicly released, which substantially undermines reproducibility and the community value of the central contribution; the checklist also contains contradictory statements ('No new assets are introduced' despite the dataset being a core asset).

The abstract claims 'state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on two popular benchmarks,' but Table 5 reports very weak zero-shot results (9.95 mIoU on NYUv2, 4.61 mIoU on OccScanNet) with no zero-shot baselines for comparison; this claim is misleading and should be revised.

Full-annotation gains are marginal and likely within run-to-run variance: +0.30 mIoU on OccScanNet and +1.04 mIoU on NYUv2, with no error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance tests (the checklist itself answers 'No error bars').

Factual inconsistencies reduce confidence: the text claims substantial OccScanNet improvements of +15.75% (tvs), +12.04% (object), and +9.95% (furniture), which do not match Table 2 (e.g., tvs improves only 50.90→51.25); section cross-references in Section 4 incorrectly point to Sections 3.1/3.2.

No ablation studies are provided: the contributions of superpixel-level vs. pixel-level distillation, the choice of VFM (SAN vs. others), the effect of pseudo-label noise from SAN, and the pipeline post-processing heuristics are not analyzed.

There is no comparison against alternative pre-training strategies (e.g., simply pre-training on OccScanNet unlabeled data, or other 2D-to-3D distillation baselines such as [4, 28]), making it hard to judge whether the gains come from the method or merely from extra data.

The dataset is modest in scale (14,592 frames from 651 clips), which sits uneasily with claims of 'large-scale' web-data learning; metric-scale recovery via the 2.8m wall-height heuristic is fragile and unvalidated.

Privacy/ethics aspects of scraping residential house-tour videos (identifiable homes/occupants) are not discussed beyond stating the data will not be released; licensing and YouTube terms-of-service considerations for scraped data are not addressed.
Writing quality issues throughout (e.g., 'collecte', 'Abstart', 'Upon on this web dataset') suggest the manuscript needed another careful pass.

strengths: Novel and meaningful problem formulation: the paper is, to the authors' knowledge, the first attempt to learn indoor 3D semantic occupancy prediction from uncalibrated in-the-wild web videos, addressing a genuine bottleneck (scarcity and cost of annotated indoor 3D data).

Complete automated pipeline (video collection/filtering, Dust3R-based geometry estimation, SAN-based open-vocabulary segmentation, voxelized occupancy generation) producing a new 100K-frame / 5,241-scene dataset with camera poses, depth, 2D semantics, and 3D occupancy pseudo-labels; the stated plan to release code and data supports reproducibility.

The paper is scientifically honest about a key negative finding: naive supervised use of the pseudo-labels yields zero-shot performance (8.41 mIoU) even below the pseudo-labels themselves, which motivates the distillation framework rather than hiding the weakness.

Model-agnostic pre-training framework with a clearly motivated dual-alignment design (voxel-anchored Gaussianization for 3D-to-2D feature rendering, plus EMA class-prototype contrastive loss), validated on three diverse architectures (CNN, Transformer, Gaussian-based) and two benchmarks with consistent gains, including new SOTA with Symphonies (+1.95 NYUv2, +1.67 Occ-ScanNet mIoU).

Thorough evaluation including comparison against alternative strategies (HASSC, GaussRender, Pri3D), few-shot analysis showing clear data-efficiency benefits (+3.29/+5.09 mIoU at 5%/10% labels on NYUv2) and a dataset-scaling trend (100K > 50K subset), plus ablations covering both losses and design variants (direct projection, learnable scale/rotation, momentum, threshold).
Limitations are explicitly discussed (occluded voxels, temporal/multi-view extension, wall-height scale assumption).
weaknesses: The claimed value of web data is partially undercut by the paper's own results: in-domain pre-training (Tab. 3) outperforms YouTube-Occ pre-training at nearly every label ratio on both benchmarks (e.g., 31.65 vs 31.45 full-data NYUv2; 49.38 vs 48.47 Occ-ScanNet). The web dataset is mainly beneficial in few-shot regimes, and the paper should temper its 'web-scale data as a promising resource' claim accordingly.

Pseudo-label quality is quantified only indirectly (raw pseudo-labels score 10.06 mIoU vs GT on Occ-ScanNet), which is very low; no error decomposition (geometry vs semantics vs scale) or per-class pseudo-label statistics are reported, making it hard to assess where pipeline improvements are most needed.

The pipeline is less 'automatic/domain-agnostic' than implied: it requires the target benchmarks' 13-class taxonomy as SAN prompts, and the 2.8 m wall-height metric-scale prior embeds a strong architectural assumption whose failure modes (rooms with different ceiling heights, non-residential scenes) are not analyzed.

Data provenance and scale details are thin: number of source videos/channels, filtering yield, deduplication, and frame/scene statistics are not reported; despite privacy being a core motivation, there is no discussion of consent/licensing/legal issues of scraping and redistributing YouTube footage, nor of person/privacy filtering.

Absolute gains on the strongest baselines are modest (EmbodiedOcc +1.04 NYUv2, MonoScene +0.93 NYUv2 with no Occ-ScanNet MonoScene result shown), and reproduced EmbodiedOcc numbers (19.14 mIoU NYUv2, 44.69 Occ-ScanNet) are far below published values (and below EmbodiedOcc++/RoboOcc), raising questions about reproduction fidelity and the fairness of some comparisons.

Some experimental details that affect reproducibility are missing or vague: pre-training duration/steps, loss weighting (L_total is an unweighted sum with no sensitivity analysis), Gaussianization rendering resolution, and how the 2D teacher/student projection handles the changed feature dimensionality at fine-tuning.

Ablation interpretations are sometimes hand-wavy (e.g., 'could indicate that our prototype-based module can alleviate noise'), and differences among loss variants (31.12 vs 31.24 vs 31.65) are small relative to typical run-to-run variance; no error bars or repeated runs are provided.

The comparison with outdoor self-supervised occupancy methods (Sec. 4.3) is qualitative only; a quantitative adaptation of at least one such method would strengthen the claim that existing approaches are infeasible for uncalibrated web video.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem setting: the paper is the first (to the authors' knowledge) to tackle indoor 3D semantic occupancy prediction from unlabeled, uncalibrated in-the-wild web videos, addressing a genuine data-scarcity and privacy bottleneck in this area.

The automated data curation pipeline (video collection, Dust3R-based geometry reconstruction, SAN-based open-vocabulary segmentation, voxelization) is a reusable contribution, and the paper promises public release of code and data, supporting reproducibility.

Honest negative analysis: Sec. 5.2 candidly shows that naive supervision with pseudo-labels fails (zero-shot 8.41% mIoU is below the raw pseudo-label quality of 10.06%), which motivates the pre-training design rather than overclaiming.

The pre-training framework is model-agnostic and validated on three heterogeneous architectures (MonoScene, Symphonies, EmbodiedOcc) across two benchmarks, with consistent though modest gains, plus a reasonable set of ablations (loss components, Gaussianization vs. direct projection, prototype momentum).

Few-shot results (Table 3) show meaningful gains in data-scarce regimes (+3.29% at 5% labels on NYUv2), which is the setting where the approach is most compelling, and a scaling trend from 50K to the full dataset is reported.
weaknesses: The headline gains are small and marginal in absolute terms: +1.95% mIoU on NYUv2 and +1.67% on Occ-ScanNet (Table 2), with gains for weaker baselines (MonoScene, EmbodiedOcc) even smaller (+0.93–1.48%). Given the large pre-training corpus (100K frames), the cost-benefit ratio of the entire pipeline is questionable.

Ambiguity about what the Table 2 'w/ Pre-training' rows are pre-trained on: the text is not explicit that pre-training uses YouTube-Occ, and the evaluation design (Sec. 5.3 point 2) is confusingly described. This is a significant clarity problem for the paper's core claim.

The pseudo-label quality is low (10.06% mIoU vs. GT), and only a handful of qualitative visualizations (Fig. 4) support the pipeline analysis. No quantitative breakdown of which failure modes (scale, semantic misalignment, occluded/invisible voxels) dominate, despite the paper attributing naive-supervision failure to two specific misalignments 'by conjecture'.

The comparison to Pri3D in Table 4 is under-argued: reporting that a published pre-training method underperforms the vanilla baseline (28.40 vs. 29.70) suggests the baselines may not be tuned or adapted fairly, weakening the 'comparison to existing strategies' evidence. HASSC/GaussRender are used as auxiliary losses rather than pre-training, making the comparison setting heterogeneous.

Several key design choices are heuristic and potentially fragile: the 2.8 m wall-height metric prior, fixed Gaussian scale/rotation, and prototype momentum; ablations exist, but no analysis of sensitivity to wall height errors or scenes violating the assumption (e.g., ceilings higher than 2.8 m), despite this being acknowledged as a limitation.

The 'first to use in-the-wild videos for 3D occupancy' claim needs more careful delineation from related 2D-to-3D pseudo-labeling and web-data reconstruction efforts; the related-work discussion is fairly thin on why existing self-supervised occupancy methods (Sec. 4.3) cannot simply be adapted.

No discussion of data licensing, copyright, or privacy implications of scraping and redistributing YouTube real-estate footage, which is a notable omission given the paper's own emphasis on privacy as motivation and its plan to publicly release the data.

Clarity issues: some notation (e.g., Eq. 1 rendering details) and the connection between pipeline pseudo-labels and the distillation framework are only loosely specified; the pre-training stage does not use the geometric pseudo-labels at all (only 2D masks/features), which should be made explicit since the pipeline's geometric products appear under-utilized.

strengths: Novel and clearly motivated problem: the paper is, to the authors' knowledge, the first to tackle indoor 3D semantic occupancy prediction from uncalibrated, in-the-wild web videos, addressing a genuine data-scarcity bottleneck for privacy-sensitive indoor environments.

The automated data curation pipeline (video collection/filtering, Dust3R-based geometry, SAN-based open-vocabulary semantics, voxelization) is well described and produces a reasonably large corpus (~100K frames, 5,241 scenes), with a promised public release of code and data supporting reproducibility.

The paper is refreshingly honest about negative results: Sec. 5.2 shows that naive supervision with pseudo-labels fails (zero-shot 8.41 mIoU, joint training degradation), which motivates the pre-training framework rather than overselling the pseudo-labels.

The dual-alignment distillation framework (voxel-anchored Gaussianization for intra-frame alignment, prototype contrastive loss for cross-scene consistency) is model-agnostic and validated on three architectures (MonoScene, Symphonies, EmbodiedOcc) across two benchmarks, with consistent gains and new SOTA with Symphonies (31.65 NYUv2, 49.38 Occ-ScanNet mIoU).

Few-shot results (Tab. 3) are the strongest evidence: +3.29/+5.09 mIoU at 5%/10% labels on NYUv2 and a clear scaling trend from 50K to the full web dataset, supporting the claim that web data provides useful 3D priors under limited supervision.

Comprehensive ablations (loss components, Gaussianization vs. direct projection, prototype momentum/threshold) and comparisons against alternative strategies (HASSC, GaussRender, Pri3D) strengthen the empirical case.
A clear limitations section identifies occluded/invisible voxels, temporal extensions, and the wall-height scale assumption.
weaknesses: The headline gains in the full-data regime are modest (+1.95 mIoU NYUv2, +1.67 Occ-ScanNet with Symphonies; around +1 or less for MonoScene and EmbodiedOcc, with no MonoScene result on Occ-ScanNet). For the model-agnostic claim, the evidence on weaker baselines is thin, and no variance/std over seeds is reported, so some gains may be within run-to-run noise.

The key attribution question is not fully resolved: the framework distills DINOv2/SAN features, so it is unclear how much of the benefit comes from the web data specifically versus the distillation objective itself. A control pre-training the same framework on other unlabeled indoor RGB-D video (e.g., ScanNet without labels) would isolate the contribution of the curated YouTube corpus; Tab. 3 actually shows in-domain NYUv2 pre-training outperforms YouTube-Occ pre-training everywhere, suggesting the web data's marginal value over accessible in-domain unlabeled data is small.

Pseudo-label quality is low (10.06 mIoU on Occ-ScanNet) and only qualitatively analyzed; there is no quantitative breakdown of geometric vs. semantic errors, no ablation of the 2.8 m wall-height prior, and the semantic teacher (SAN) both generates the pseudo-labels and supervises distillation, creating a possible circularity the paper does not analyze.

Table 1 raises concerns about the pipeline itself: zero-shot transfer (8.41) is below the pseudo-labels' own quality (10.06) and naive joint training degrades the NYUv2 baseline, meaning the collected data is only usable through the proposed distillation—practical utility beyond this particular pre-training recipe is untested.
The 2.8 m wall-height assumption is a crude metric-scale heuristic that could bias scenes with non-standard geometry (lofts, commercial spaces); the impact on the pseudo-labels is not quantified.

Dataset provenance and legality are under-addressed: scraping YouTube real-estate videos raises copyright, terms-of-service, and privacy questions, and the real-estate domain biases the data toward a narrow scene distribution (furnished, static, empty-ish rooms), which is acknowledged only implicitly through the video-source rationale.

Some technical details are underspecified for reproducibility: opacity MLP design, rendering resolution, region-mask handling of classes absent from a frame, negative-pair construction in Eq. 2 across batch elements, and filtering thresholds; the crawl itself is hard to reproduce exactly.

No evaluation of whether the pre-training transfers to other tasks (detection, segmentation) or to truly out-of-domain scenes, so the 'generalizable 3D priors' claim rests solely on the two occupancy benchmarks that share the same taxonomy as the pseudo-labeling prompts.
